transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-03-28
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~42 minutes
Attendees: Alex Chen (Redwood AE), Priya Nair (Redwood SE), Mark Rivera (Verdant IT Lead), Sasha Kim (Verdant InfoSec), Jamal Ortiz (Verdant CTO)

Summary:
Short discovery focused on Verdant's requirements for a Private/VPC deployment of Redwood, networking constraints (VPC peering, private endpoints), region/residency needs, and security controls. Next steps captured for docs, network details, and follow-up deep dive.

Topics: private VPC topology, peering vs PrivateLink, egress controls, KMS integration, region constraints, pilot timeline

Transcript:
[00:00] Alex Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, uh we'll do quick intros. I'm Alex, AE on the account.
[00:05] Mark Rivera: Hi Alex, Mark here, I run infra at Verdant.
[00:07] Sasha Kim: Sasha, security.
[00:09] Jamal Ortiz: Jamal, CTO.
[00:11] Priya Nair: Priya from Redwood, I handle the SE side for Private deployments.
[00:15] Alex Chen: Great. The goal for today is to understand your constraints for Private/VPC and how Redwood's Private offering maps to that. We'll cover peering, private endpoints, region and compliance questions.
[00:29] Mark Rivera: Cool, to set context Verdant's prod workloads live in us-east-1 and we have a strict policy that nothing goes over public internet. We prefer VPC peering but open to PrivateLink if peering causes problems. Latency is pretty important for our chat assist product, so sub-50ms to our apps would be ideal.
[00:48] Sasha Kim: From security: SOC2 is baseline, we need audit logs, KMS integration for at-rest encryption, and SSO/SAML for access. Also we have a requirement for dedicated tenant isolation for PII workloads.
[01:05] Priya Nair: Understood. Quick note on Redwood Private: we provide a customer-controlled VPC peering model and a private endpoint model. For peering, we peer Redwood's VPC to yours in the same region, routing through AWS backbone — traffic stays within AWS. For private endpoints, we can offer endpoint services (PrivateLink) so you connect to an endpoint service in your VPC. Both support KMS/HSM integrations, and we surface audit logs to your logging bucket or S3.
[01:38] Jamal Ortiz: What's the tradeoff between peering and PrivateLink for us?
[01:42] Priya Nair: Good question. VPC peering is straightforward and lower latencies because it's VPC-to-VPC routing; however, peering requires non-overlapping CIDRs and we need IAM+route tables set up. PrivateLink avoids route table changes and is more controlled in terms of allowed services, but can add additional egress hops and, depending on region, slightly higher latency. From a security posture PrivateLink is often preferred by InfoSec teams.
[02:10] Mark Rivera: Our CIDRs are 10.10.0.0/16 and 10.20.0.0/16 for prod and staging.
[02:15] Sasha Kim: We also have an egress proxy that forces all outbound to go through a NAT and is scanned. Any solution needs to be compatible.
[02:22] Priya Nair: We can support environments with outbound egress — customers either allow peered traffic to flow directly, or they force egress through their proxy, in which case we'd recommend routing rules that allow traffic to Redwood endpoints via the proxy IPs. We have docs with example route tables and proxy configs.
[02:40] Alex Chen: On region constraints, Jamal mentioned us-east-1 — do you have any other region residency needs?
[02:47] Jamal Ortiz: We have some customers in EU requiring data residency, but our initial rollout will be in us-east-1. We may need EU later. How fast can Redwood spin up a private instance in eu-west-1?
[02:58] Priya Nair: We can provision Private control planes in eu-west-1 but it adds lead time — typically 4-6 weeks depending on capacity and compliance checks. For Dedicated reserved capacity we can often provision faster if we have pool availability. For multi-region, we can offer separate control planes per region to keep data residency boundaries clean.
[03:18] Sasha Kim: For auditability, can we get ingestion of syslogs and per-request audit logs? We need to feed to our SIEM.
[03:25] Priya Nair: Yes, we stream audit logs (request metadata, model version, user token id) to your S3/Kinesis endpoint; we also have retention controls. We'll share the log schema and sample messages.
[03:37] Mark Rivera: What about KMS? We use AWS KMS with custom key policies, and for some datasets we need HSM-backed keys.
[03:44] Priya Nair: Redwood supports customer-managed KMS keys. For HSM-backed keys we have integration patterns; for fully on-prem HSMs we support hybrid approaches but there are additional security reviews.
[03:55] Alex Chen: Any blockers on your side for peering? Overlapping CIDRs? Firewall rules?
[04:00] Mark Rivera: CIDRs are not overlapping, but our compliance team requires traffic be restricted to specific ports and TLS only.
[04:05] Sasha Kim: Also need RBAC mapping to our SAML groups.
[04:09] Priya Nair: We support SSO with SAML/OIDC and can map SAML groups to Redwood roles. RBAC can be enforced at the console and API keys. We'll add SAML integration steps to the docs.
[04:20] Jamal Ortiz: Latency — you said peering gives low latency. Any benchmarks?
[04:24] Priya Nair: We collect per-route latency metrics. From us-east-1 peered setups we typically see median token-latency improvements of 10-25% compared to public endpoints — in practice that's often tens of milliseconds. We can run a quick benchmark during a pilot if you want us to spin up a test endpoint and you run load from your app nodes.
[04:43] Mark Rivera: Yes we'd want to run a benchmark. Also curious about fallback. If a region fails, do you have automatic fallback to hosted models?
[04:51] Alex Chen: We support routing policies — you can configure a failover to either a hosted Redwood endpoint in another region or to a different model variant. But for private workloads customers often prefer explicit failover policies.
[05:02] Sasha Kim: For PII workloads we want to ensure no data leaves our VPC. How do you guarantee that?
[05:07] Priya Nair: For Private with peering, traffic stays in the AWS backbone between your VPC and our VPC; we don't route payloads through public internet. For Dedicated/private on-prem we can host the inference runtime in your VPC or on-premise which ensures data never leaves. We'll include an architecture diagram.
[05:25] Mark Rivera: Do you support private ECR repositories for model images or do you push images from Redwood side?
[05:30] Priya Nair: For Private deployments we can pull images from your private ECR or we can provide signed images; generally customers prefer us to pull from a customer-controlled ECR for higher control. We'll outline options.
[05:40] Jamal Ortiz: Compliance: what's in the security pack? SOC2, ISO, pen test reports?
[05:45] Alex Chen: We'll share SOC2 and ISO attestations plus a redacted pen test summary. Priya will attach the security pack to the follow-up.
[05:52] Sasha Kim: Network-level question: will you require cross-account roles for peering setup?
[05:56] Priya Nair: We usually request a cross-account role with limited permissions to create peering attachments and route table changes, but many customers prefer to perform the peering from their side and just accept the peering request. Either model is supported.
[06:10] Mark Rivera: We prefer to accept the peering request, our network team won't hand out broad perms.
[06:14] Alex Chen: Noted. For egress and NAT — since you have enforced outbound, we'll provide sample NAT and proxy configurations.
[06:20] Mark Rivera: For the pilot, what does the onboarding look like?
[06:23] Priya Nair: Onboarding for a Private pilot: 1) exchange network details (CIDRs, subnets, NACLs), 2) set up peering or PrivateLink, 3) configure routing and test connectivity, 4) provision a small dedicated pool or private instance and run benchmarks, 5) validate logs and KMS integration, 6) sign-off and scale. Typically a 2-6 week pilot depending on internal approvals.
[06:48] Jamal Ortiz: Budget and cost question: what's the cost delta between Redwood Hosted and Private?
[06:53] Alex Chen: Private includes additional costs for the control plane and dedicated deployment resources; Dedicated reserved pools are priced differently. We'll send a TCO that compares per-token costs plus fixed infra. We'll include assumptions for batch sizes and KV cache use since those materially change unit costs.
[07:10] Mark Rivera: One more networking nuance — we have multiple AWS accounts (prod, staging) behind an AWS Transit Gateway. Can you peer to a TGW?
[07:18] Priya Nair: We can peer to a VPC that's attached to your TGW; depending on routing we may need specific route propagation. We have done TGW patterns with customers and will share a sample diagram.
[07:30] Sasha Kim: Ok, sounds good. Action items and next steps?
[07:33] Alex Chen: Recap: we'll send network peering doc, security pack, sample configs, and a proposed timeline. Priya will own the deep-dive demo for networking. Mark will share CIDRs and a list of subnets. We'll schedule the pilot kickoff pending those artifacts.
[07:50] Mark Rivera: Sounds good. Thanks everyone.
[07:52] Jamal Ortiz: Thanks, appreciate it.
[07:54] Alex Chen: Thanks all, we'll follow up by end of week.

End of transcript.
